content: The World Health Organization (WHO) is a specialized agency of the United Nations (UN) that serves as the coordinating authority on international public health. It was established on April 7, 1948, and is headquartered in Geneva, Switzerland. The WHO inherited its mandate and resources from its predecessor, the Health Organization of the League of Nations. The WHO's constitution defines its primary objective as achieving the highest possible level of health for all people. Its main responsibilities include combating diseases, particularly infectious diseases, and promoting the overall health of populations worldwide. The WHO was one of the original agencies of the United Nations. Its constitution came into effect on April 7, 1948, which is celebrated as World Health Day. Before its formal establishment, its operations were managed by an Interim Commission following an International Health Conference in 1946. The transfer of responsibilities from the League of Nations' Health Organization to the WHO was authorized by a UN General Assembly resolution. The WHO coordinates international efforts to monitor and respond to outbreaks of infectious diseases such as SARS, malaria, and AIDS. It also sponsors programs to prevent and treat these diseases. The organization supports the development and distribution of safe and effective vaccines, diagnostics, and medications. Notably, after more than two decades of effort, the WHO declared smallpox eradicated in 1980, marking the first disease in history to be eliminated through human intervention. The WHO is also working on vaccines for malaria and schistosomiasis and aims to eradicate polio in the near future. The WHO has endorsed the world's first official HIV/AIDS Toolkit for Zimbabwe, setting an international standard. Beyond disease eradication, the organization conducts health-related campaigns, such as promoting fruit and vegetable consumption and discouraging tobacco use. In February 2007, experts at WHO headquarters in Geneva reported significant progress in developing pandemic influenza vaccines, with over 40 clinical trials completed or ongoing. These trials, initially focused on healthy adults, have expanded to include children and the elderly. All tested vaccines have been found to be safe and well-tolerated across age groups. The WHO also conducts research on various health topics, including the potential health effects of electromagnetic fields from cell phones. Some of this work has been controversial, such as the joint WHO/FAO report in April 2003 recommending that sugar intake should not exceed 10% of a healthy diet. In addition to its stated mission, the WHO has responsibilities assigned by international treaties. For example, under the Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs and the Convention on Psychotropic Substances, the WHO provides binding scientific and medical assessments of psychoactive drugs and recommends their regulation. The organization also compiles the International Classification of Diseases (ICD), with the 10th revision released in 1992 and later versions available online and in print. The WHO maintains a model list of essential medicines that all countries' healthcare systems should make accessible and affordable. The WHO's supreme decision-making body is the World Health Assembly, which consists of delegations from its 193 member states. The Assembly meets annually in May to appoint the Director-General, review financial policies, and approve the program budget. It also elects 34 members to the Executive Board for three-year terms. The Board's main functions include implementing Assembly decisions, advising the Assembly, and facilitating its work. The WHO has 193 member states, including all UN member states except Liechtenstein, and two non-UN members, Niue and the Cook Islands. Territories not recognized as UN member states can join as Associate Members with limited participation and voting rights. Examples include Puerto Rico and Tokelau. Entities like the Palestine Liberation Organization and the Holy See have observer status. The WHO is funded by contributions from member states and donors. In recent years, voluntary contributions from governments, foundations, NGOs, other UN organizations, and the private sector have exceeded assessed contributions from member nations. The organization collaborates with around 80 partners, including NGOs, the pharmaceutical industry, and foundations like the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation. The WHO operates six regional offices, each with significant autonomy. These offices are led by Regional Directors elected for five-year terms by their respective Regional Committees. The Regional Committees set guidelines for implementing WHO policies within their regions and review the organization's progress. The Regional Directors oversee staff and country offices within their regions. The WHO has 147 country and liaison offices worldwide, typically located in capitals and sometimes accompanied by satellite offices. These offices are headed by WHO Representatives, who are trained physicians with diplomatic rank. Their main functions include advising governments on health and pharmaceutical policies. Liaison offices serve similar purposes on a smaller scale and are often found in countries with fewer health system challenges. The WHO has partnerships with private sector organizations, including PATH, the International AIDS Vaccine Initiative, Medicines for Malaria Venture, and others. These collaborations focus on developing and distributing health technologies and treatments. The WHO publishes the annual World Health Report, which provides expert assessments of global health and focuses on specific topics. The 2007 report, A Safer Future: Global Public Health Security in the 21st Century, was published on August 23, 2006. The WHO's health statistics are widely regarded as impartial, global, and technically competent. These statistics influence national and international resource allocation, policymaking, and programming. The WHO has faced controversies, such as its relationship with the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA). Critics argue that this agreement has limited the WHO's ability to address the health effects of ionizing radiation, particularly in the aftermath of the Chernobyl disaster. Former WHO Director-General Dr. Hiroshi Nakajima admitted that documents on the disaster's effects were censored due to the agreement with the IAEA. Protests against this agreement have been ongoing since April 27, 2007.
